title: Set a new teammate up to win
goal: You will create a reusable first-week onboarding project covering accounts, tools, first tasks, and check-ins.
prerequisites: An Asana account with permission to create projects
The new hire's name, manager, start date, and email
A list of required accounts and tools

steps.action: Create a blank project named "New Hire Onboarding – Template".
steps.where: Left sidebar Create button, then Project, Blank project dialog.
steps.why: A dedicated template keeps the onboarding process consistent and reusable.
steps.checkpoint: The project header shows "New Hire Onboarding – Template" in List view.
hint_levels: Start from the creation control in the sidebar.
Choose a project rather than a task, then select the blank-project option.
Click Create > Project > Blank project, enter "New Hire Onboarding – Template", choose List, then click Create project.

steps.action: Add sections named "Before Day 1", "Accounts & Access", "Tools & Setup", "First Tasks", and "Check-ins".
steps.where: Project List view, Add section control above the task list.
steps.why: Sections organize the checklist by onboarding stage and responsibility.
steps.checkpoint: All five section headings appear in the project task list.
hint_levels: Look above the task rows for the section control.
Create one section for each onboarding stage, preserving the requested order.
Click Add section, type each section name, press Enter, and repeat until all five appear.

steps.action: Add preparation tasks under "Before Day 1" for sending the welcome email, confirming the start schedule, and assigning a buddy.
steps.where: Project List view, task rows beneath the "Before Day 1" section heading.
steps.why: Completing preparation early prevents avoidable first-day delays.
steps.checkpoint: Three separate task rows appear under "Before Day 1".
hint_levels: Add the work as separate rows beneath the first section.
The three task names should begin with clear verbs: Send, Confirm, and Assign.
Click Add task under Before Day 1, enter each task name, and press Enter after each one.

steps.action: Add one task for each required account under "Accounts & Access".
steps.where: Project List view, task rows beneath the "Accounts & Access" section heading.
steps.why: Separate account tasks make missing access visible and assignable.
steps.checkpoint: Every required account appears as its own task in the Accounts & Access section.
hint_levels: Turn each login or permission into its own task.
Use names such as "Create email account" and "Grant shared-drive access" rather than one combined access task.
Click Add task under Accounts & Access, type one account action, press Enter, and repeat for every account.

steps.action: Add one installation or configuration task for each required tool under "Tools & Setup".
steps.where: Project List view, task rows beneath the "Tools & Setup" section heading.
steps.why: A tool-by-tool list makes setup progress easy to verify.
steps.checkpoint: Each required tool has a separate setup task visible under Tools & Setup.
hint_levels: Use the tools list you gathered before starting.
Phrase each row as an observable setup action, such as "Sign in to Slack" or "Clone the team repository".
Under Tools & Setup, click Add task, enter one tool setup action, press Enter, and repeat for the remaining tools.

steps.action: Add three outcome-based starter tasks under "First Tasks".
steps.where: Project List view, task rows beneath the "First Tasks" section heading.
steps.why: Small real deliverables help the new hire learn the workflow while contributing.
steps.checkpoint: Three distinct deliverables appear under First Tasks, each beginning with an action verb.
hint_levels: Choose small pieces of genuine team work.
Make each task produce a visible result, such as updating a profile, completing a practice ticket, or submitting a small change.
Click Add task under First Tasks, type the first deliverable, press Enter, and repeat until three tasks are listed.

steps.action: Add Day 1, Day 3, and Day 5 manager check-in tasks under "Check-ins".
steps.where: Project List view, task rows beneath the "Check-ins" section heading.
steps.why: Scheduled touchpoints surface access problems and unclear expectations early.
steps.checkpoint: The Check-ins section shows three separate tasks labeled Day 1, Day 3, and Day 5.
hint_levels: Create a beginning, middle, and end-of-week conversation.
Name each task with both its day and purpose, such as "Day 3 check-in: unblock setup and first tasks".
Under Check-ins, add three tasks named "Day 1 check-in", "Day 3 check-in", and "Day 5 check-in", pressing Enter after each.

steps.action: Assign every checklist task to the role responsible for completing it.
steps.where: Project List view, Assignee column beside each task row.
steps.why: Explicit ownership prevents onboarding work from falling between the manager, IT, buddy, and new hire.
steps.checkpoint: Every task row displays an assignee avatar or name in the Assignee column.
hint_levels: Scan the assignee column for empty cells.
Use the actual responsible teammate where possible and a role placeholder in the template where needed.
Click each empty Assignee cell, search for and select the responsible person, then continue until no task is unassigned.

steps.action: Convert the finished project into an Asana template.
steps.where: Project header dropdown beside the project name, Save as template option.
steps.why: A project template lets the team launch the same onboarding structure for every new hire.
steps.checkpoint: Asana displays the saved template in the team's Templates gallery.
hint_levels: Use the project-level menu near its title.
The reuse command is in the project header dropdown and is labeled Save as template.
Click the dropdown beside "New Hire Onboarding – Template", select Save as template, complete the template details, then click Create template.
